title: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current

questions.chapter: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of $N$ turns, radius $R$, carrying current $I$ is:
questions.solution:
$B = \mathbf{\dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2R}}$ at the centre of a circular coil.

Every element of the loop is at the same distance $R$ from the centre and contributes in the same direction, which is why the integration is so simple.

Do not confuse it with the field of a **long straight wire**, $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi R}$ — the geometry is different and so is the $\pi$.

questions.chapter: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field along the field direction. Its path is:
questions.solution:
$\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ has magnitude $qvB\sin\theta$. Moving **along** the field means $\theta = 0$, so the force is zero and the particle continues in a **straight line** undeflected.

Perpendicular entry gives a **circle**; entry at any other angle gives a **helix**, since the parallel component is unaffected while the perpendicular component circles.

questions.chapter: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: In a moving coil galvanometer, the radial magnetic field is produced by concave pole pieces so that:
options: The deflection is proportional to the current
questions.solution:
With a **radial** field, the plane of the coil is always **parallel** to the field whatever its position, so $\sin\theta = 1$ at every angle and the torque is $NIAB$ rather than $NIAB\sin\theta$.

At equilibrium $NIAB = k\phi$, so

$\phi \propto I$

The scale is therefore **linear and uniform**. Without the radial field the deflection would vary as $\sin\theta$ and the scale would be cramped at one end.

questions.chapter: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: The angle between the geographic meridian and the magnetic meridian at a place is called the:
questions.solution:
**Declination** is the horizontal angle between the geographic and magnetic meridians — it says how far a compass needle points away from true north.

**Dip** (or inclination) is the **vertical** angle the needle makes with the horizontal. It is $0^\circ$ at the magnetic equator and $90^\circ$ at the poles.

Together with the horizontal component $B_H$, these three are the **elements of the Earth's magnetic field**.

questions.chapter: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: A diamagnetic material placed in a non-uniform magnetic field moves:
questions.solution:
Diamagnetic materials are **feebly repelled** by a magnetic field, so they move from the stronger to the **weaker** region.

Their susceptibility is small and **negative**, and they have no permanent atomic dipole moment — the induced moment opposes the applied field, which is Lenz's law at the atomic scale.

Paramagnetic and ferromagnetic materials are attracted towards the stronger region instead. Bismuth, copper and water are diamagnetic, which is how a frog has been levitated in a strong field.

questions.chapter: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: The magnetic field inside a long solenoid of $n$ turns per unit length carrying current $I$ is:
questions.solution:
$B = \mathbf{\mu_0 nI}$ inside a long solenoid, where $n$ is turns **per unit length**.

The field is **uniform** along the axis and essentially **zero outside**, which is what makes a solenoid the standard way of producing a known uniform field.

At the **ends** it falls to half this value, $\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_0 nI$, because only half the solenoid contributes there.

questions.chapter: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: The magnetic moment of a current loop of area $A$ carrying current $I$ with $N$ turns is:
questions.solution:
$m = \mathbf{NIA}$, directed perpendicular to the plane of the loop by the right-hand rule.

This is why a current loop behaves as a **magnetic dipole**: it experiences a torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{m}\times\vec{B}$ in a field, exactly as a bar magnet does, and it is the basis of the moving coil galvanometer and the electric motor.

questions.chapter: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: Above the Curie temperature, a ferromagnetic material becomes:
questions.solution:
Above the **Curie temperature** the thermal agitation destroys the alignment within the magnetic **domains**, and the material becomes **paramagnetic**.

It does not become non-magnetic altogether — the atomic dipoles survive, they simply no longer align cooperatively.

For iron the Curie point is $1043\ \text{K}$. Above it the susceptibility follows the Curie-Weiss law, $\chi \propto \dfrac{1}{T - T_C}$.

questions.chapter: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: The work done by a magnetic force on a moving charged particle is:
questions.solution:
The magnetic force $q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ is **always perpendicular to the velocity**, so $\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v} = 0$ and the work done is **always zero**.

A magnetic field can therefore change a particle's **direction** but never its **speed** or kinetic energy — which is exactly why a cyclotron needs an electric field to accelerate the particle and uses the magnetic field only to bend it round.

questions.chapter: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: What is the angle of dip, in degrees, at the magnetic equator?
questions.solution:
At the magnetic equator the Earth's field is **horizontal**, so the dip needle rests horizontally and the angle of dip is $\mathbf{0^\circ}$.

At the magnetic poles the field is vertical and the dip is $90^\circ$. Since $B_H = B\cos\delta$, the horizontal component is greatest at the equator and zero at the poles.

questions.chapter: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
questions.q: Describe the construction and working of a moving coil galvanometer, deriving the relation between current and deflection. Explain the purpose of the radial magnetic field, and describe how the instrument is converted into an ammeter and into a voltmeter.
questions.solution:
**Construction.** A rectangular coil of $N$ turns of fine insulated wire is wound on a light non-magnetic frame and suspended by a **phosphor bronze strip** between the **concave pole pieces** of a permanent horseshoe magnet. A soft iron **cylindrical core** sits inside the coil without touching it. A mirror on the suspension allows the deflection to be read by a lamp and scale.

**Working.** When a current $I$ flows, the coil — a magnetic dipole of moment $NIA$ — experiences a **deflecting torque** in the field:

$\tau_{\text{def}} = NIAB\sin\theta$

As the coil turns, the suspension wire twists and exerts a **restoring torque** proportional to the angle of twist:

$\tau_{\text{res}} = k\phi$

where $k$ is the torsional constant. The coil settles where the two balance.

**Deriving the relation.** At equilibrium, with the radial field ensuring $\sin\theta = 1$:

$NIAB = k\phi$

$\boxed{I = \left(\dfrac{k}{NAB}\right)\phi}$

or equivalently $\phi = \left(\dfrac{NAB}{k}\right)I$, so $\phi \propto I$.

The quantity $\dfrac{k}{NAB}$ is the **galvanometer constant** or figure of merit — the current needed for unit deflection.

**The purpose of the radial field, which is the point of the design.**

The concave pole pieces together with the soft iron core produce a **radial** field: the field lines run along radii, so that **whatever position the coil takes, its plane is always parallel to the field**.

This matters because it makes $\theta$ always $90^\circ$ between the normal to the coil and the field, so $\sin\theta = 1$ **at every deflection**.

Without it the torque would be $NIAB\sin\theta$ and the relation would be $I \propto \dfrac{\phi}{\sin\theta}$ — a **non-linear** scale, cramped at one end and stretched at the other, which would have to be individually calibrated rather than simply divided into equal parts.

The soft iron core does a second job as well: being highly permeable, it concentrates the field lines and so **increases** $B$, making the instrument more sensitive.

**Sensitivity.** Current sensitivity is $\dfrac{\phi}{I} = \dfrac{NAB}{k}$. It is raised by increasing $N$, $A$ or $B$, or by reducing $k$ — which is why a phosphor bronze strip is used, having a very small torsional constant.

But increasing $N$ and $A$ also increases the coil's **resistance**, and voltage sensitivity is $\dfrac{\phi}{V} = \dfrac{NAB}{kR}$. So **raising the current sensitivity does not necessarily raise the voltage sensitivity** — a genuinely useful point, and the reason the two are quoted separately.

**Conversion into an ammeter.**

An ammeter goes in **series** and must therefore have **low** resistance, and must carry a large current the delicate coil cannot take.

A **low resistance $S$, called a shunt, is connected in parallel** with the galvanometer, so most of the current bypasses the coil.

If $I_g$ is the full-scale galvanometer current and $I$ the current to be measured, the parallel voltages are equal:

$I_gG = (I - I_g)S \Rightarrow S = \dfrac{I_gG}{I - I_g}$

The combination has resistance $\dfrac{GS}{G+S}$, which is **less than $S$** and so very small — as required, since an ideal ammeter has zero resistance and would not disturb the circuit it measures.

**Conversion into a voltmeter.**

A voltmeter goes in **parallel** and must therefore have **high** resistance, so that it draws as little current as possible from the circuit.

A **high resistance $R$ is connected in series** with the galvanometer.

For a full-scale reading $V$:

$V = I_g(G + R) \Rightarrow R = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G$

The combination has resistance $G + R$, which is large — as required, since an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

**The symmetry is worth noticing.** Both conversions start from the same instrument and go in opposite directions: **low resistance in parallel** for the series instrument, **high resistance in series** for the parallel one. In each case the added resistance is chosen so that the galvanometer still receives exactly $I_g$ at full scale, and in each case it moves the instrument's total resistance towards the ideal value that disturbs the circuit least.
